description: Hi! I’m creating a team for the Field Shift challenge. I’m looking for motivated teammates. You don’t need to be an expert, beginners are welcome! I’m looking for people who are curious, willing to learn, communicate well, and want to build something meaningful together.
summary:
FieldTank is a desktop pixel-art farming game that shows how crop and irrigation decisions play out under real weather. Players act as Sam, a farmer, across five real seasons. After picking a goal (maximize yield, save water, or avoid plant stress), they choose a crop (maize, soybean or sorghum), with or without irrigation. The game animates the season, showing soil-water levels every 3 days, heat and crop condition, then compares the choice with the best option for that goal. Poor choices cost hearts, and a final tally shows how close the player came to the best plan.

Every number is read from a data file: the game never invents agronomic values and uses no randomness. The data is based on a simplified daily soil-water balance using Daymet weather and gNATSGO soil data (Hargreaves ET0, FAO-56 crop coefficients, FAO relative yield). An optional panel shows a 20x20 GOES-16 surface-temperature grid, labelled as an example. In-game Assumptions and Credits screens state the limits: yield is relative, and this is a simulation, not agronomic advice.

Built with Python and pygame, with automated tests and CC0 art.
details:
What it does and how it works:

FieldTank is a desktop pixel-art farming game. The player is Sam, a farmer, who lives through five real-world seasons. Every season is a decision: which crop to sow (maize, soybean or sorghum) and whether to irrigate. The game then shows what happened.

A run goes like this:

  1. Choose a goal. Maximize yield, save water, or avoid plant stress. The goal sets the scoring: yield alone, yield minus 0.4 × irrigation (mm), or yield minus 1.5 × stress days.
  2. Read the season. Each season opens with its rain, number of hot days, soil water capacity and latitude, taken from the data file.
  3. Answer the question. The five questions are: which crop without irrigation, whether to irrigate the maize, which crop with irrigation, whether to irrigate the soybean, and finally all six crop-and-irrigation options.
  4. Watch the season play out. for about eight seconds. A soil-water tank shows the water level every 3 days from sowing. The soil changes between healthy, dry and cracked, and crops, heat and irrigation drops animate accordingly.
  5. See the result. A chart compares the chosen water curve with the best option for the player's goal, next to the raw numbers: yield, stress days, heat days and irrigation volume.
  6. Hearts. A choice within 10 points of the best costs nothing, within 30 costs one heart, and anything worse costs two. If all five hearts are lost, the farm fails. Otherwise a final tally compares the total score with the best possible plan and shows Sam's mood.

Data and method:

The game never invents agronomic numbers and uses no randomness. Every outcome is read from a validated data file: five scenes, six choices each. If the file is missing or malformed, the game shows an error screen instead of running on made-up values. Option order is shuffled with a fixed seed, so every run is reproducible.

The scenes are based on a simplified daily soil-water balance with Daymet weather and gNATSGO soil data, Hargreaves reference evapotranspiration, FAO-56 crop coefficients and the FAO relative-yield method. Initial soil water is 80% of capacity. Irrigation applies 25 mm automatically when stress begins, up to 100 mm per season. The model's stress threshold is 50% of capacity. The heat penalty (1% yield per day above the crop's threshold) is our own assumption, not part of FAO, and the game says so.

An optional panel shows a 20×20 land-surface-temperature grid from a GOES-16 satellite snapshot, with hover read-out in °C and K and an outline around the hottest 10% of pixels. It is labelled as an example, not data from the season being played.

Benefits:

  • Water and heat decisions are hard to grasp from tables. The game lets players see why irrigation helps in some years and wastes water in others.
  • The scoring changes with the goal, so players learn that "best" depends on what you value: yield, water or crop health.
  • Every number on screen is traceable to the data file, so the game can be checked and not just trusted.

Intended impact:

We want players to understand water trade-offs in farming through short, immediate feedback loops, using real seasonal data instead of invented examples. The design can take new locations and seasons: swapping the data file is enough to run the game on another place, with no code change.

Tools, languages, hardware and software:

  • Language: Python 3.
  • Game engine: pygame-ce, with a fixed 1280×720 logical screen that scales to any window size and supports fullscreen.
  • Data: JSON files with strict validation. The satellite grid is optional.
  • Testing: pytest, covering data validation, scoring, heart loss, question filtering and shuffling.
  • Packaging: PyInstaller for a standalone executable.
  • Art: the CC0 Tiny Farm pack by Kenney. A Pillow script rebuilds the tiles, crops and farmer mood sprites from the original tilemap.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on an ordinary computer.
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub.

How it is creative:

  • Real data becomes a small story. Sam asks a question, the player chooses, and consequences are shown on the soil, the tank and Sam's face.
  • The same season gives different lessons depending on the goal the player picked.
  • The game shows its own limits. In-game Assumptions and Credits screens list the method and sources, and results display the raw file values behind each outcome.

Factors our team considered:

  • Honesty about data: no invented numbers, relative yield instead of fake tonnes or prices, and a clear statement that this is a simulation, not agronomic advice.
  • Reproducibility: fixed shuffle seed, deterministic outcomes, and automated tests.
  • Safety against mistakes: the loader refuses test fixtures, and invalid data stops the game with a readable error.
  • Accessibility and reach: keyboard and mouse controls, a bilingual English/French interface, and a window that resizes cleanly.
  • Scope: five seasons, three crops and two irrigation choices keep each decision understandable while still showing real trade-offs.
